questions.question: What are Pods, Deployments, Services, and ConfigMaps in Kubernetes and how do they relate?
questions.title: Kubernetes Core Objects: Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap
questions.direct_answer: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit — one or more containers sharing network and storage. A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet which keeps a desired number of Pods alive, handling rolling updates and rollbacks. A Service gives that dynamic set of Pods a stable virtual IP and DNS name via a label selector. A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration injected into Pods as env or mounted files. Together they form a layered abstraction with reconciliation loops keeping actual state equal to declared state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the Kubernetes abstraction hierarchy and why each object exists separately
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking a Pod is just another word for container, or managing Pods directly instead of via Deployment and missing self-healing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the controller reconciliation loop, the Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod indirection that enables rolling updates, how Services discover Pods via label selectors and endpoint objects, and what triggers a ConfigMap-driven restart

sections.title: The Misconception That Costs You the Interview: Pods Are Not Containers
sections.content:
Most developers first learning Kubernetes assume a Pod is just another word for a container. That model breaks the first time they try to run a sidecar proxy alongside their Spring Boot app — both containers must share network and lifecycle, and that shared boundary is the Pod. Understanding the four core objects — Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap — as **layers of abstraction** rather than standalone things is what separates a developer who uses `kubectl` from one who understands what it does.

- **A Pod wraps one or more containers** into a single scheduling unit. Containers in the same Pod share `localhost` networking and can mount the same volumes. They start and stop together. Pods are ephemeral: a node fails and the Pod is gone forever unless a controller is watching.
- **A Deployment** declares desired state and a controller loop keeps actual state matching it. This is the layer where self-healing lives.
- **A Service** gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name over a dynamic set of Pods, resolved by label selector.
- **A ConfigMap / Secret** injects configuration at Pod startup, keeping image and config separate.

The real question interviewers probe: why exist as separate abstractions? The answer is **separation of concerns**. Each owns one job and they compose through **label selectors**.

sections.title: The Abstraction Hierarchy and Its Reconciliation Loop
sections.content:
Each object is declarative — you write the desired state, a controller drives the cluster toward it. The Deployment controller watches for drift between desired and actual, creating or deleting objects as needed.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    User[kubectl apply\nDeployment.yaml] --> API[Kube API Server]
    API --> DC[Deployment Controller]
    DC -->|creates/updates| RS[ReplicaSet\nreplicas=3]
    RSC[ReplicaSet Controller] -->|observes| RS
    RSC -->|creates| P1[Pod 1]
    RSC -->|creates| P2[Pod 2]
    RSC -->|creates| P3[Pod 3]
    SVC[Service\nselector: app=order] -. label match .-> P1
    SVC -. label match .-> P2
    SVC -. label match .-> P3
    EP[Endpoints\nauto-updated] --> SVC
    CM[ConfigMap] -. envFrom / volume .-> P1
    KP[kube-proxy\niptables / IPVS] --> SVC
    Client[Other Pod\norder-service.ns.svc] --> KP
```

The Deployment creates and manages a **ReplicaSet**; the ReplicaSet manages Pods. Services do not manage Pods at all — they reference them via labels. The **Endpoints** object is continuously rebuilt by the control plane to reflect which Pods currently match the Service's selector and are passing readiness.

sections.title: The Controller Loop That Makes Deployments Self-Healing
sections.content:
The Deployment controller runs a continuous **reconciliation loop**: compare desired state (3 replicas of image v2.1) with actual state (2 pods running, 1 crashed) then act (create 1 replacement). This loop runs constantly, not just at deploy time.

When you create a Deployment it does not manage Pods directly. It creates a **ReplicaSet** — an intermediate object whose only job is maintaining N identical replicas. The Deployment manages ReplicaSets, and ReplicaSets manage Pods. This two-layer indirection exists for **rolling updates**: changing the image tag creates a new ReplicaSet for the new version and scales down the old one, both alive during transition.

This is the insight interviewers want. Pods crash, nodes fail, resources get preempted — none of it requires human intervention because the controller detects drift and corrects it. A **ConfigMap follows a different pattern**: it stores non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs that Pods reference, but it has no controller loop of its own. Updating a ConfigMap does not restart Pods unless you add explicit machinery (e.g., Spring Cloud Kubernetes, a checksum annotation, or Reloader).

sections.title: How Services Discover Pods Whose IPs Change on Every Restart
sections.content:
Every Pod gets a unique IP, but that IP is **ephemeral** — it changes on every restart, reschedule, or scale event. If `order-service` hardcoded the IP of `payment-service`, it would break the moment Kubernetes moved the payment Pod.

**Services solve this with label selectors.** A Service says: route traffic to any Pod carrying `app: payment-service`. Kubernetes maintains an **Endpoints** object listing current IPs of matching healthy Pods, updated in real time as Pods come and go. Other services call the DNS name — `payment-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local` — which resolves to a stable ClusterIP. **kube-proxy** on each node translates that virtual IP to an actual Pod IP using iptables or IPVS rules.

**The most common misconfiguration is a label mismatch.** The Service's `spec.selector` does not match the Pod template's labels. Endpoints is empty and every request fails with `connection refused` or DNS timeout. Diagnose instantly with:

```bash
kubectl get endpoints <service-name>      # empty = label mismatch
kubectl get pods --show-labels             # confirm actual Pod labels
```

Readiness probe failures produce the same symptom: the Pod exists but is excluded from Endpoints until it is ready.

sections.title: Trade-offs, Anti-patterns, and When to Reach for More
sections.content:
**When not to use a Deployment.** Deployments are right for stateless services. If each replica needs stable identity and its own persistent storage (databases, Kafka, ZooKeeper), use a **StatefulSet**. For node-level agents (log shippers, metric collectors) use a **DaemonSet** — one Pod per node, no count management.

**ConfigMap vs Secret.** ConfigMap is not encrypted. Put database passwords, API keys, and TLS certs in Secrets. Secrets are base64-encoded at rest; combine with RBAC (only the namespace can read) and **etcd encryption-at-rest** for real protection. For high-security environments, use a Secrets Store CSI driver to pull from AWS Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault and never persist secrets in the cluster at all.

**Rolling ConfigMap updates.** Changing a ConfigMap does not restart Pods by default. Three common solutions: (1) embed a `checksum/config` annotation in the Pod template so any config change rolls the Deployment, (2) use **Reloader** operator to watch ConfigMaps and trigger rollouts, (3) use **Spring Cloud Kubernetes** to watch in-process and refresh beans with `@RefreshScope`.

**Service type choice is a cost question.** `ClusterIP` (internal only) is free. `NodePort` exposes on every node port. `LoadBalancer` allocates a cloud load balancer per Service — one LB per microservice gets expensive fast. Prefer a single **Ingress** fronting many Services, or a **ServiceMesh** (Istio, Linkerd) for north-south and east-west traffic with one entry point.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Pod wraps containers, is not equal to container** — one Pod can run an app + sidecar sharing localhost and volumes; Pods are the scheduling unit, not containers.
- **Deployment controller runs a continuous reconciliation loop** — it compares desired vs actual every few seconds and replaces crashed Pods automatically.
- **ReplicaSet is the hidden middle layer** — Deployments do not manage Pods directly; rolling updates scale up a new ReplicaSet while scaling down the old one.
- **Services discover via label selectors, not hardcoded IPs** — the selector must match Pod labels; `kubectl get endpoints <svc>` shows zero IPs on a mismatch.
- **ConfigMap updates do not restart Pods automatically** — use checksum annotations, Reloader, or Spring Cloud Kubernetes to trigger reloads on config change.
- **Secrets for sensitive data, plus RBAC and etcd encryption** — base64 is not encryption; pair Secrets with access control and at-rest encryption for real protection.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
In Kubernetes you never manage individual containers directly — you work with abstractions that the control plane continuously reconciles toward your declared desired state. The four you interact with constantly are Pod, Deployment, Service, and ConfigMap, and they form a hierarchy: Deployments manage ReplicaSets which manage Pods, Services route traffic to Pods by label selector, and ConfigMaps inject configuration at startup.

**Pod — the smallest deployable unit**
- A Pod wraps one or more containers that share a network namespace and storage volumes — they communicate over localhost and share the same IP; you rarely create Pods directly in production for this reason.
- Pods are ephemeral by design: when a node fails or a Pod is deleted, it is gone; the Deployment controller creates a replacement Pod, typically with a new IP — nothing should depend on a Pod's IP address directly.
- The Pod spec sets resource requests and limits, liveness/readiness probes, environment variables, and volume mounts — all the container-level configuration lives here.

**Deployment — the controller that keeps Pods running**
- A Deployment declares desired state: "run 3 replicas of `payment-service:v2.1`" — the controller loops continuously comparing actual versus desired and creates or deletes Pods to close any gap.
- Under the hood, Deployments manage ReplicaSets — when you update the image tag, a new ReplicaSet is created and scaled up while the old one scales down; this two-layer design enables zero-downtime rolling updates.
- `kubectl rollout undo deployment/payment-service` reverts to the previous ReplicaSet in seconds; Kubernetes keeps a configurable revision history (default 10) specifically for this.

**Service — stable network identity for ephemeral Pods**
- Pods get new IPs on every restart, so nothing should route to a Pod IP directly; a Service creates a stable virtual IP (ClusterIP) and DNS name — `payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local` — that survives Pod restarts.
- The Service uses a label selector to find its target Pods; `kubectl get endpoints payment-service` shows which Pod IPs are currently behind the selector.
- Ingress sits in front of Services to terminate TLS and route HTTP by host or path to different backends — the Service itself handles TCP load balancing, not HTTP-layer routing.

**ConfigMap — configuration separate from image**
- ConfigMaps inject configuration via `envFrom` for env vars or as mounted files; separating config from image means the same image runs in dev, staging, and prod with different ConfigMaps.
- Updating a ConfigMap does not restart Pods automatically — use a `checksum/config` annotation on the Pod template or a tool like Reloader to trigger a rolling update on config change.
- Use Secrets for sensitive data like database passwords and API keys — Secrets are base64 at rest which is not encryption; combine with RBAC and etcd encryption-at-rest for real protection.

questions.question: What is the difference between liveness, readiness, and startup probes in Kubernetes for Spring Boot?
questions.title: Kubernetes Probes: Liveness vs Readiness vs Startup for Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Liveness answers 'is the process stuck?' — failure restarts the container. Readiness answers 'can this pod serve traffic now?' — failure removes it from Service endpoints without restart. Startup answers 'has the app finished initializing?' — while failing, both liveness and readiness are suspended. Use all three for Spring Boot: startup covers slow boot, readiness tracks dependency health, liveness catches only unrecoverable deadlocks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand different failure behaviors and when each probe type is needed
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Omitting startup probe for Spring Boot — liveness fires during JVM startup, container restarts, loop repeats forever; OR putting DB checks in liveness so a brief DB outage restarts every pod simultaneously
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Spring Boot `/actuator/health/liveness` vs `/readiness` split, the restart-loop scenario, how ApplicationAvailability API emits signals, and why dependency checks belong in readiness not liveness

sections.title: The Restart Loop That Kills Every Spring Boot Deploy Without a Startup Probe
sections.content:
Spring Boot takes 45 seconds to initialize — loading the context, running Flyway migrations, warming caches. You deploy with a liveness probe set to check every 10 seconds after a 30-second delay. The probe fires at second 30, the app is not ready, fails three times, and Kubernetes restarts the container. The new container starts initializing and the cycle repeats forever. **Your deployment never completes.**

This **restart loop** is the single most common Kubernetes failure for Spring Boot teams. It exists because of a fundamental confusion between three probe types that look similar but trigger completely different behaviors. Liveness, readiness, and startup probes each answer a different question about container health, and each produces a different failure action.

The **startup probe** was added to Kubernetes specifically to solve this. It acts as a guard that holds off liveness and readiness checking until the application signals it has finished initializing. Without it, you are stuck guessing `initialDelaySeconds` — and guessing wrong means either restart loops or delayed detection of genuinely stuck pods.

sections.title: The Three Probes Over a Pod's Lifetime
sections.content:
Timing matters. Startup is active only during boot. Readiness gates Service routing continuously. Liveness catches unrecoverable states.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant K as kubelet
    participant P as Pod (Spring Boot)
    participant S as Service endpoints
    K->>P: startupProbe /health/liveness (t=0)
    P-->>K: 503 (Context loading)
    K->>P: startupProbe (t=10s, 20s, 30s...)
    P-->>K: 503 (Flyway running)
    K->>P: startupProbe (t=50s)
    P-->>K: 200 OK (UP)
    Note over K: Startup succeeded\nLiveness & readiness now enabled
    K->>P: readinessProbe /health/readiness
    P-->>K: 200 OK
    K->>S: Add pod IP to Endpoints
    Note over K,S: Traffic starts flowing
    K->>P: livenessProbe (every 10s)
    K->>P: readinessProbe (every 5s)
    P-->>K: Readiness 503 (DB pool exhausted)
    K->>S: Remove pod from Endpoints
    Note over P: Pod still running\nRecovers when DB reconnects
    P-->>K: Readiness 200 OK
    K->>S: Re-add pod to Endpoints
```

Notice liveness was never triggered — the DB blip removed the Pod from traffic but did not restart it. That is the correct separation.

sections.title: Three Questions With Three Different Consequences
sections.content:
The distinction is not mechanism — all three can use HTTP, TCP, or exec checks. The distinction is **what Kubernetes does when the probe fails**.

| Probe | Question It Answers | On Failure | On Success | Typical Check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Liveness | Is the process stuck or deadlocked? | Restart the container | No action | Shallow: is JVM responding? |
| Readiness | Can this pod serve requests right now? | Remove from Service endpoints | Add to endpoints | Dependency health: DB pool, cache, downstream |
| Startup | Has the application finished initializing? | Keep waiting (restart only after threshold) | Enable liveness & readiness | Same as liveness but long window |

**Liveness should detect unrecoverable states** — deadlocks, corrupted state, crashed event loops. It should **never check external dependencies** because a temporary DB outage would restart every pod simultaneously, turning a partial outage into a total one.

**Readiness is the right probe for dependency health.** When the DB connection pool is exhausted, readiness fails, the pod stops receiving traffic, and when the pool recovers readiness passes again — all without a restart.

The **startup probe** runs exclusively during initialization and suspends both liveness and readiness until it succeeds. Configure it with `failureThreshold * periodSeconds = maximum startup time`. Once it passes, it never runs again.

sections.title: Mapping Spring Boot Actuator to Probe Configuration
sections.content:
Spring Boot 2.3+ provides dedicated endpoints aligned with Kubernetes health checks:

- `/actuator/health/liveness` — fails only if the app marks itself `BROKEN` via `ApplicationAvailability.getLivenessState()`.
- `/actuator/health/readiness` — fails when Spring detects unavailable dependencies (DB, cache); transitions to `ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC` after `ApplicationReadyEvent`.

The Deployment maps directly. The sizing decision that matters is the startup window: `failureThreshold * periodSeconds`.

```yaml
startupProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080}
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 10    # 30 * 10s = 5 minute startup window
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080}
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3  # 3 * 10s = 30s stuck before restart
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080}
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3  # 3 * 5s = 15s unhealthy before drop from endpoints
```

Note the absence of `initialDelaySeconds` — the startup probe makes it unnecessary and this pattern adapts to varying boot times. Spring Boot 3.x enables the probe endpoints automatically when it detects a Kubernetes environment; in 2.x set `management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true`.

sections.title: Trade-offs, Anti-patterns, and Tuning
sections.content:
**Never check DB in liveness.** Every team eventually learns this the hard way. A brief PostgreSQL primary failover takes 30 seconds. During that window, if liveness checks DB connectivity, every pod across every replica fails liveness, every pod restarts, and the outage triples in blast radius.

**Readiness should be smart about recovery.** Readiness failures pull the pod from traffic but keep it running so it can recover in place. A pod that flaps between ready and not-ready causes load-balancer churn. Use `failureThreshold: 3` with `periodSeconds: 5` so a single flaky check does not immediately disrupt traffic; pair with a circuit breaker inside the app so dependency blips are absorbed internally rather than surfaced to readiness.

**Startup probe `failureThreshold` must exceed real P99 boot time.** Measure actual boot with `Started Application in X seconds` log line across many deploys and use P99 + 30% margin. A 120s P99 boot needs `failureThreshold: 20` at `periodSeconds: 10` (200s window).

**Exec probes are expensive.** They fork a process inside the container — for a JVM in a tight memory cgroup, this can cost real memory. Prefer HTTP probes unless you must shell out.

**Probes vs observability.** Probes tell Kubernetes what to do automatically. They do not replace alerting on SLOs. A pod oscillating between ready and not-ready for a dependency outage is working correctly at the probe level — but your on-call still needs a Prometheus alert on `kube_pod_status_ready == 0 for 5m` to know humans need to look.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Liveness failure restarts; readiness failure removes from load balancer** — mixing these causes either unnecessary restarts during DB blips or continued traffic to pods that cannot serve requests.
- **Startup probe prevents the restart loop** — without it a Spring Boot app taking 45s to start gets killed by liveness set at 30s, creating infinite restart cycles that block deployment.
- **Never check dependencies in liveness** — a brief DB failover fails every pod's liveness simultaneously and converts a partial outage into a total cluster-wide outage.
- **`failureThreshold * periodSeconds` = startup window** — set to P99 boot time + 30% margin instead of guessing `initialDelaySeconds` on the liveness probe.
- **Spring Boot Actuator splits liveness from readiness** — liveness only fails when the app marks itself `BROKEN`; readiness fails and recovers automatically with dependency availability; `ApplicationAvailability` API emits transitions.
- **Probes automate, alerts inform** — probes keep the system recovering without humans; still alert on sustained `kube_pod_status_ready == 0` so on-call knows when recovery isn't happening.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kubernetes uses three probe types to determine container health, and they exist for different failure modes. Misconfiguring them — particularly confusing liveness with readiness — causes either cascading restarts that bring down a healthy application or traffic being sent to containers that are not ready.

**Liveness — is the JVM responding?**
- A failed liveness check restarts the container; it is the circuit breaker for deadlocked, hung, or permanently broken processes that cannot recover without a restart.
- Use the Actuator liveness endpoint: `GET /actuator/health/liveness` — Spring Boot 2.3+ reports `UP` when the context is healthy and not broken; it does not check database connectivity because a database outage should not restart healthy Pods.
- Set a generous window via startup probe rather than `initialDelaySeconds` — a liveness probe that fires during Spring Boot's init triggers a restart loop.

**Readiness — is the app ready for traffic?**
- A failed readiness check removes the Pod from the Service's Endpoints; traffic stops routing to it, but the Pod keeps running and can recover; this is the correct response to temporary overload or slow downstream dependencies.
- Use `GET /actuator/health/readiness` — Spring Boot's readiness state starts as `REFUSING_TRAFFIC` during init and transitions to `ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC` only after `ApplicationReadyEvent` fires, including database connection pool establishment.
- Set readiness `failureThreshold` lower than liveness — failing quickly removes a pod from rotation; liveness requires more failures before triggering restart to avoid restarting a slow-but-recovering pod.

**Startup — protecting slow-starting JVMs**
- The startup probe is the correct solution for slow Spring Boot apps; while it has not succeeded, liveness and readiness checks are suspended — this prevents the restart loop during initialization.
- `failureThreshold: 30` with `periodSeconds: 10` gives the app 5 minutes to start; after startup succeeds, liveness and readiness take over with normal thresholds.
- Without a startup probe you must inflate liveness `initialDelaySeconds` — that delay also applies after real restarts, making recovery slower than necessary.

**Anti-patterns to avoid**
- Dependency checks in liveness turn a partial outage into a total one — a 30-second DB failover restarts every pod across every replica simultaneously.
- Exec probes on memory-tight JVM pods are expensive — they fork processes inside the container; prefer HTTP probes unless you must shell out.

questions.question: How do you set resource requests and limits for a JVM application in Kubernetes?
questions.title: Kubernetes Resource Requests and Limits for JVM Apps
questions.direct_answer: Memory: set `requests` to steady-state usage and `limits` to a safe ceiling (~1.5x heap). Use `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` with `-XX:+UseContainerSupport` so heap tracks the cgroup limit automatically. CPU: set requests to typical usage; be cautious with CPU limits — they cause CFS throttling that freezes all JVM threads including GC. For latency-critical services, use Guaranteed QoS (requests == limits) on memory; often leave CPU limits unset for Burstable flexibility.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand how Kubernetes resource management interacts with JVM memory, threads, and GC
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting memory limit = `-Xmx` (ignoring metaspace, thread stacks, code cache) causing deterministic OOMKills; or setting aggressive CPU limits that throttle GC and inflate P99
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain QoS classes (Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort), CFS throttling effect on GC pauses, Vertical Pod Autoscaler in recommend mode, and why `-Xmx` + `-Xms` equal avoids runtime heap resize pauses

sections.title: The Silent Killer: JVM Heap Equal to the Container Memory Limit
sections.content:
The most predictable OOMKill in Kubernetes: set container memory limit to 1Gi, configure `-Xmx1g`, watch the pod get killed within hours. The JVM needs **more memory than just heap** — metaspace for loaded classes (100–200MB for a typical Spring Boot app), thread stacks (1MB per thread times 200+ Tomcat threads), JIT code cache (50–100MB), GC overhead, NIO direct buffers. Setting `-Xmx` equal to the limit leaves zero room for any of these, and the cgroup kills the process the moment total RSS exceeds the limit.

This is the single most common JVM-on-Kubernetes failure and it stems from a **mental-model mismatch**. In traditional deployments the JVM was the only significant process and could negotiate with the OS. In a container the **cgroup memory limit is a hard ceiling** enforced by the kernel. There is no negotiation — exceed by a byte and the OOM killer fires immediately.

The fix: use `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` instead of a fixed `-Xmx`. This caps heap at 75% of the container's available memory, leaving 25% for non-heap. For a 1Gi limit, heap maxes at ~768MB with ~256MB reserved for everything else.

sections.title: Memory Footprint of a JVM Container
sections.content:
The container memory limit covers every byte the JVM process consumes — not just heap. The chart below shows a typical Spring Boot pod at 1Gi limit.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Container[Container cgroup limit = 1 Gi]
        direction TB
        Heap[Heap\n-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75%\n~ 768 MB]
        NonHeap[Non-Heap Total\n~ 256 MB]
        subgraph NH[Non-Heap breakdown]
            Meta[Metaspace\n120 MB]
            Stacks[Thread Stacks\n200 × 1 MB]
            Code[Code Cache\n50 MB]
            GC[GC overhead\n20 MB]
            Direct[Direct Buffers\nNetty / NIO]
        end
    end
    NonHeap --> NH
    Limit[cgroup kills process if\nRSS > 1 Gi] -.-> Container
```

The 75% ratio is calibrated: 25% of 1Gi (256MB) comfortably covers 120MB metaspace + 200MB thread stacks + JIT cache + GC overhead for a typical service. High-thread or Netty-heavy apps may need a lower percentage (65–70%).

sections.title: Memory Sizing: Why 75% Is the Right Heap-to-Container Ratio
sections.content:
The `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` flag works with `-XX:+UseContainerSupport` (enabled by default since Java 10) which makes the JVM read cgroup memory limits instead of host memory. Together, heap scales automatically with whatever limit you set on the container.

The 75% ratio is not arbitrary. A typical Spring Boot non-heap breakdown: metaspace 100–200MB (Spring's reflection-heavy model loads thousands of classes), thread stacks 1MB each (Tomcat default 200 threads = 200MB), code cache 50–100MB, plus GC working memory and direct buffers. The remaining 25% of 1Gi (~256MB) covers these with safety margin.

```yaml
env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: >-
      -XX:+UseContainerSupport
      -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0
      -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0
resources:
  requests: {memory: 512Mi, cpu: 250m}
  limits:   {memory: 1Gi,   cpu: 1000m}
```

**Requests** drive scheduling — the scheduler ensures the node has 512Mi free before placing the pod. **Limits** drive enforcement — exceeding 1Gi triggers OOMKill. The gap between requests and limits defines **QoS class**: equal values produce `Guaranteed` (never evicted under pressure), unequal values produce `Burstable` (evicted before Guaranteed pods). For a 3-replica Deployment, set `requests.memory = limits.memory` so all replicas have guaranteed memory — JVMs behave badly when swapped or squeezed.

sections.title: CPU Throttling Damages P99 Latency With No Visible Error
sections.content:
Memory limit violations are dramatic: exit 137 and restart. **CPU limit violations are silent and insidious.** When a container exceeds its CPU quota, the Linux CFS scheduler **pauses the entire cgroup** until the next scheduling period. The JVM stops — all threads frozen — and resumes when the quota refills.

This throttling manifests as latency spikes impossible to diagnose from app logs alone. The JVM does not know it was paused. GC that should take 20ms takes 200ms because GC threads were frozen mid-cycle. A request that should complete in 5ms takes 50ms because the CPU quota was exhausted by concurrent GC. Your P99 graph shows unexplained spikes while P50 looks normal.

The **diagnostic key** is the Prometheus metric:

```promql
rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total{pod="$pod"}[5m])
  / rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{pod="$pod"}[5m])
```

If throttled ratio exceeds 5% of total CPU time, either raise the CPU limit or remove it entirely. Many production teams **remove CPU limits** and keep only requests — this gives Burstable QoS with freedom to burst during GC pauses and JIT compilation. The scheduler still uses requests for placement so resources are reserved; only the enforcement ceiling is removed.

For latency-critical services where predictability trumps flexibility, set requests equal to limits for Guaranteed QoS. The scheduler reserves exactly those resources, pod is last to evict under node pressure, and throttling is tuned rather than removed.

sections.title: QoS Classes, VPA, and Sizing Strategies
sections.content:
**QoS classes** are derived from your requests/limits, not declared explicitly. They determine eviction order under node pressure.

| QoS | Condition | Eviction Priority | When to Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Guaranteed | requests == limits on both CPU and memory | Last to evict | Latency-critical services, JVMs |
| Burstable | requests < limits (any resource) | Middle | Most services, good cluster packing |
| BestEffort | No requests or limits | First to evict | Never in production |

**`-Xmx` and `-Xms` equal.** For latency-critical JVMs, set `-Xmx` and `-Xms` equal (via `MinRAMPercentage = MaxRAMPercentage`) so the heap does not resize at runtime. Heap resize triggers full GC pauses that can hit hundreds of milliseconds — unacceptable for a payment service.

**Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA)** observes actual usage over days and recommends adjusted requests/limits. Run VPA in `recommend` mode first so you review suggestions before enabling automatic resizing — `auto` mode restarts pods on resize which causes production churn. VPA is excellent for initial sizing discovery but dangerous when left to adjust continuously.

**Requests tuning is capacity planning.** Setting requests too low lets the scheduler pack many JVMs onto one node; they all ramp up under load, everyone OOMKills simultaneously. Setting requests too high wastes capacity across the cluster (capacity is reserved even when idle). The right baseline is steady-state usage from VPA recommendations, plus 20% headroom.

**Observability you must add.** Alert on `container_memory_working_set_bytes / container_spec_memory_limit_bytes > 0.85 for 10m` as the OOMKill early warning. Alert on CFS throttled ratio > 5% for 15m as the CPU-throttling early warning. Both fire before the incident, not during the post-mortem.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`-Xmx` must never equal the container memory limit** — metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, GC overhead need 200–400MB beyond heap; setting equal guarantees OOMKill within hours.
- **`MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` + `UseContainerSupport`** — JVM reads cgroup limits and sets heap to 75% of container memory automatically; scales without hardcoded `-Xmx`.
- **CPU throttling causes invisible latency spikes** — CFS pauses the cgroup when quota is exhausted including GC threads; P99 spikes while P50 looks normal and no errors appear in logs.
- **Requests drive scheduling, limits drive enforcement** — requests pick the node; memory limits OOMKill, CPU limits throttle without termination.
- **QoS: Guaranteed (requests == limits) for latency-critical** — last-to-evict under node pressure; Burstable gives better packing but can be evicted; BestEffort first to die.
- **`-Xmx` and `-Xms` equal avoids heap-resize GC pauses** — latency-critical JVMs should not see runtime resize; set min and max to the same value via matching RAMPercentage flags.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kubernetes resource requests and limits are the two numbers the scheduler and kubelet use to decide where to place Pods and when to kill them. Getting them wrong for a JVM is one of the most common causes of OOMKilled pods and degraded cluster scheduling.

**Requests — scheduling guarantees**
- `resources.requests` tells the scheduler how much CPU and memory the pod needs — the scheduler places the pod on a node that has at least this much available; if no node has enough, the pod stays Pending.
- Requests define the Pod's QoS class: requests == limits gives Guaranteed (last to evict); requests < limits gives Burstable; no requests at all gives BestEffort (first to evict).
- Set memory requests based on actual idle JVM footprint from `kubectl top pod` during normal operation; setting requests too low packs too many JVMs onto one node and they all OOMKill together when traffic hits.

**Limits — enforcement ceilings**
- `resources.limits.memory` is a hard ceiling enforced by cgroups — exceed and the kernel OOMKills; no warning, no JVM cleanup.
- Set memory limits to at least 1.3–1.5x the heap (`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`) to account for metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers — a JVM with 512MB heap needs at least 700–800MB total container limit.
- CPU limits throttle using cgroup CPU quota — a JVM hitting the limit slows down but is not killed; excessive throttling (visible in `container_cpu_throttled_seconds_total`) degrades GC performance because GC threads are also throttled.

**Recommended settings**
- Set `requests.memory == limits.memory` for Guaranteed QoS — JVMs have unpredictable memory footprints and should not compete with other pods; predictable allocation is worth the lost burst capacity.
- Leave CPU limits unset or set generously — CPU throttling degrades latency under load without meaningful protection; use CPU requests for scheduling placement without CPU limits for execution.
- For latency-critical services, set `-Xmx` and `-Xms` equal via matching RAMPercentage flags — this avoids full-GC pauses that happen when the heap resizes at runtime.

**Observability**
- Alert on `container_memory_working_set_bytes / limit > 0.85 for 10 minutes` as an OOMKill early warning.
- Alert on CFS throttled ratio > 5% for 15 minutes to catch CPU-throttling-induced latency before it shows up in the user experience.
- Use Vertical Pod Autoscaler in `recommend` mode to discover correct sizing empirically over days — review suggestions before enabling automatic resizing.

questions.question: How do rolling updates and rollbacks work in Kubernetes Deployments?
questions.title: Kubernetes Rolling Updates and Rollbacks
questions.direct_answer: Rolling updates replace pods incrementally — new pods start, pass readiness, then old pods are terminated. Behavior is controlled by `maxSurge` (extra pods above desired) and `maxUnavailable` (pods allowed offline). `maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0` guarantees zero downtime. Kubernetes retains old ReplicaSets (up to `revisionHistoryLimit`, default 10) so `kubectl rollout undo` is instant and requires no image rebuild. For higher-risk changes, blue-green and canary are safer alternatives to native rolling.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how Kubernetes achieves zero-downtime deployments
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Omitting `maxUnavailable: 0` (allows pods terminated before replacements ready) or missing readiness probes (bad pods receive traffic)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Kubernetes keeps the previous ReplicaSet for rollback, discuss `revisionHistoryLimit`, mention PodDisruptionBudget during node drains, and compare rolling to blue-green and canary for risk reduction

sections.title: Why `maxUnavailable: 0` Is the Only Setting That Guarantees Zero Downtime
sections.content:
A rolling update sounds simple: replace old pods with new ones gradually. But the default settings do not guarantee zero downtime. The Kubernetes default is `maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 25%` — Kubernetes can terminate 25% of your pods before replacements are ready. For a 4-replica Deployment, one pod is killed before the new version is running. During that window, capacity is reduced and requests may drop if load is high.

**Zero downtime requires `maxUnavailable: 0` explicitly.** This tells Kubernetes to never terminate an old pod until a new one has passed its readiness probe. Combined with `maxSurge: 1`, the Deployment creates one extra pod running the new version, waits for it to become ready, then terminates one old pod. **Capacity never drops below desired count.**

The mechanism that makes this work is the **ReplicaSet**. When you change a Deployment's pod template (usually the image tag), the Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet for the new version. Both ReplicaSets exist simultaneously during transition — new scaling up, old scaling down. Kubernetes keeps the old ReplicaSet around (scaled to zero replicas) after rollout completes, which is what makes **instant rollback** possible.

sections.title: The Rollout Sequence With maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0
sections.content:
On a 4-replica Deployment, the rollout proceeds in lock-step: add one, wait for ready, remove one, repeat.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as User
    participant D as Deployment Controller
    participant RS1 as ReplicaSet v1 (4 pods)
    participant RS2 as ReplicaSet v2 (new)
    participant K as kubelet
    U->>D: kubectl set image app=v2
    D->>RS2: Create, desired=1
    RS2->>K: Create pod v2-1
    K-->>RS2: Ready (readiness 200)
    D->>RS1: Scale to 3
    RS1->>K: Terminate pod v1-4 (graceful)
    D->>RS2: Scale to 2
    RS2->>K: Create pod v2-2
    K-->>RS2: Ready
    D->>RS1: Scale to 2
    Note over D: ...repeats...
    D->>RS2: Scale to 4 (final)
    D->>RS1: Scale to 0 (kept for rollback)
    Note over RS1: ReplicaSet v1 retained\nper revisionHistoryLimit
```

**Readiness probes are the quality gate.** If the new version fails readiness, the rollout stalls — old pods keep serving traffic indefinitely until you fix forward or `kubectl rollout undo`.

sections.title: The Rollout Dance: New ReplicaSet Scales Up While Old Keeps Serving
sections.content:
`kubectl set image deployment/spring-app app=myapp:v2` (or applying an updated manifest) causes the Deployment controller to create a new ReplicaSet for v2 and begin scaling it up.

```yaml
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1
    maxUnavailable: 0
progressDeadlineSeconds: 600
```

With 4 replicas the sequence: create v2-1 (total 5), wait for ready, terminate one v1 (total 4), create v2-2 (total 5), repeat until all 4 pods run v2.

**`progressDeadlineSeconds`** is the timeout — if the rollout has not completed in 600s, the controller marks it `Failed`. This does NOT automatically roll back — you still get stuck pods and old pods serving. Check with:

```bash
kubectl rollout status deployment/spring-app
kubectl rollout history deployment/spring-app
kubectl describe deployment spring-app   # shows ReplicaSet status
```

If readiness keeps failing — bad migration, misconfigured env, upstream dependency unavailable — the rollout stalls with the new pod in `0/1 Running` and old pods keep serving. This is intentional: Kubernetes protects you from shipping a broken version.

sections.title: Rollback Is Instant Because the Old ReplicaSet Is Never Discarded
sections.content:
The most powerful aspect of Kubernetes rollback is what it does not do: rebuild images, re-download layers, re-run CI. `kubectl rollout undo deployment/spring-app` simply scales the previous ReplicaSet back up and scales the current one down. Old pods' image references are still in the ReplicaSet spec — Kubernetes pulls from cache and starts pods immediately.

This works because the Deployment retains old ReplicaSets up to **`revisionHistoryLimit`** (default 10). Each ReplicaSet records the exact pod template used: image tag, env vars, resource limits. Rolling back to revision 3 means scaling up the existing ReplicaSet that already has that spec.

```bash
kubectl rollout history deployment/spring-app
# REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
# 7         Image updated to v2.1.0
# 8         Image updated to v2.1.1
# 9         Image updated to v2.2.0   <-- broken

kubectl rollout undo deployment/spring-app
# reverts to revision 8

kubectl rollout undo deployment/spring-app --to-revision=7
# skip intermediate revision
```

If the rollback itself fails readiness, the same protection applies — old pods keep serving while the system waits.

**`revisionHistoryLimit` tuning:** default 10 is fine for most Deployments. For high-frequency releases (several per day), raise to 20–50 to preserve rollback depth. For cost-sensitive clusters where etcd storage matters, lower to 5.

sections.title: Rolling vs Blue-Green vs Canary: Risk vs Cost Trade-offs
sections.content:
Native rolling updates have a **mixed-version window** — for several minutes old and new pods serve traffic simultaneously. For most backend services this is fine. For incompatible database schema changes or breaking API contracts, it is catastrophic.

| Strategy | Capacity Overhead | Rollback Speed | Good For | Not Good For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rolling | +maxSurge (e.g., +25%) | Fast (old RS retained) | Most backend services | Breaking schema changes |
| Blue-Green | 2x (both environments up) | Instant (flip Service) | High-risk releases, DB migrations | Cost-constrained clusters |
| Canary | +1 pod (canary replica) | Progressive traffic shift | Risk-reducing large changes | Simple services (overkill) |

**Blue-green.** Deploy v2 as a completely separate Deployment (`spring-app-blue` vs `spring-app-green`). Verify in isolation with internal traffic. Flip the Service's label selector atomically (`app: payment, version: green`) to switch 100% traffic in one kubectl command. Rollback = flip back. Cost: **2x compute** during the switchover.

**Canary.** Deploy a small number of v2 pods alongside v1 (e.g., 1 canary + 9 stable). Weight traffic with an Ingress / service-mesh (Istio VirtualService) at 10% to canary. Monitor error rate and latency. If healthy, progressively shift to 50% → 100%. **Ecosystem tools**: Flagger, Argo Rollouts automate this with Prometheus-based analysis.

**PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) still matters during rolling.** A `kubectl drain` on a node during unrelated maintenance evicts pods. Without a PDB, a 3-replica Deployment could lose all 3 pods on one node simultaneously. `minAvailable: 2` forces evictions one at a time.

**`maxSurge` costs capacity.** The cluster must have room for the extra pods during rollout. On tight clusters, consider `maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1` — trades brief capacity reduction for no capacity overhead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`maxUnavailable: 0` is required for zero downtime** — the 25% default allows pods to terminate before replacements are ready, briefly reducing capacity below the desired count.
- **Readiness probes gate the rollout** — failed probes stall the rollout and old pods keep serving; without probes, broken deployments immediately receive traffic.
- **Rollback reuses existing ReplicaSets** — `kubectl rollout undo` scales up the previous ReplicaSet without rebuilding images; old pod specs are retained up to `revisionHistoryLimit`.
- **`progressDeadlineSeconds`** marks a stalled rollout `Failed` but does NOT auto-rollback — you still have stuck pods; `kubectl rollout undo` is manual.
- **PodDisruptionBudget protects voluntary disruptions** — without it a node drain during cluster upgrade can evict all replicas at once; `minAvailable: 2` keeps service up.
- **Blue-green for breaking schema, canary for risk-reducing large changes** — rolling updates have a mixed-version window; when that window is unsafe, pick a strategy that eliminates or controls it.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kubernetes rolling updates replace running Pods incrementally — new Pods start before old Pods terminate, maintaining availability throughout the deployment. The two parameters that control update speed and risk are `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable`.

**Rolling update mechanics**
- `maxSurge: 1` allows one pod above the desired replica count during rollout — with 3 replicas, Kubernetes starts one new Pod (4 total), waits for it to pass readiness, terminates one old Pod; this continues until all pods run the new version.
- `maxUnavailable: 0` ensures zero pod downtime — no old pod terminates until its replacement passes readiness; set this to 0 in production for services that cannot tolerate reduced capacity during deploys.
- The readiness probe is the critical coupling: a broken new version where readiness never passes stalls the rollout — old pods keep serving, the broken new pod sits in `0/1 Running`, and the rollout never progresses; this is a feature, not a bug.

**Triggering and monitoring**
- `kubectl set image deployment/payment-service app=payment-service:v2.1.0` triggers a rolling update — Kubernetes records this as a new revision in the rollout history.
- `kubectl rollout status deployment/payment-service` blocks and streams progress until all replicas are on the new version or `progressDeadlineSeconds` (default 600s) elapses.
- `kubectl rollout history deployment/payment-service` shows revision history; annotate `kubernetes.io/change-cause` on updates so the history is meaningful.

**Rollback**
- `kubectl rollout undo deployment/payment-service` reverts to the previous ReplicaSet immediately — old pods are recreated from the previous spec; no image rebuild required.
- `kubectl rollout undo deployment/payment-service --to-revision=3` rolls back to a specific revision — useful when the last version is also broken.
- `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10) controls how many old ReplicaSets are kept; setting it too low means you cannot roll back past recent releases.

**When rolling is not enough**
- For breaking database schema changes, use blue-green — deploy v2 as a separate Deployment, verify in isolation, flip the Service selector atomically to switch traffic, flip back for rollback.
- For high-risk large changes, use canary — deploy one or two pods alongside the stable version, weight 10% of traffic to them via Ingress or service mesh, monitor error rate, progressively shift to 100%.
- Always pair rolling with a PodDisruptionBudget — `minAvailable: 2` prevents node drains from evicting all replicas simultaneously during cluster maintenance.

questions.question: When do you need StatefulSets and PersistentVolumes in Kubernetes?
questions.title: StatefulSets and PersistentVolumes for Stateful Java Services
questions.direct_answer: StatefulSets are for workloads where each replica is not interchangeable — stable network identity (`postgres-0` remains `postgres-0`), stable per-replica storage (each pod gets its own PVC via `volumeClaimTemplates`), and ordered operations. Databases, Kafka, Elasticsearch need this. **Most Spring Boot services are stateless and belong on Deployments** — even those that use a database. PersistentVolumes provide durable storage provisioned dynamically via StorageClass and survive Pod deletion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know when NOT to use StatefulSets (most Spring Boot apps are stateless)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running a database as a Deployment — random pod names, shared PVC or no PVC, split-brain or data loss; or deleting a StatefulSet and expecting PVCs to go with it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the three StatefulSet guarantees (stable ID, stable storage, ordered operations), when managed DBs (RDS, Cloud SQL) are better, VolumeClaimTemplates, headless Services, and `WaitForFirstConsumer` binding mode

sections.title: The Decision That Reveals Kubernetes Experience: When NOT to Use StatefulSets
sections.content:
The quickest way an interviewer gauges Kubernetes experience is asking when to use a StatefulSet versus a Deployment. Junior candidates reach for StatefulSets because the name suggests anything with "state" needs one. Experienced engineers know **most Spring Boot apps are stateless and belong on Deployments** — even if they use a database. The application stores its state in PostgreSQL; the application itself has no state that differs between replicas.

StatefulSets exist for workloads where **each replica is not interchangeable** — databases, message brokers, distributed data stores where every instance has a unique identity and its own persistent storage. A PostgreSQL primary must know it is the primary. A Kafka broker registered as `kafka-0` must remain `kafka-0` after restart so partition assignments stay valid. A Redis Cluster node must rejoin with the same data.

These requirements — **stable network identity, stable persistent storage, ordered startup and shutdown** — are the three guarantees that only StatefulSets provide. Deployments treat all pods as interchangeable: random names, random IPs, shared or no persistent storage. If your app fits that model, a Deployment is simpler, faster to scale, easier to manage. **Decision framework:** interchangeable replicas → Deployment; each replica has a unique role that must survive restarts → StatefulSet.

sections.title: StatefulSet With VolumeClaimTemplates and Headless Service
sections.content:
Each StatefulSet pod gets a stable name, a stable DNS entry via the headless Service, and its own PVC from the template.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    SS[StatefulSet\nname: postgres\nreplicas: 3] --> P0[Pod postgres-0]
    SS --> P1[Pod postgres-1]
    SS --> P2[Pod postgres-2]
    SS -.volumeClaimTemplate.-> PVC0[PVC data-postgres-0]
    SS -.volumeClaimTemplate.-> PVC1[PVC data-postgres-1]
    SS -.volumeClaimTemplate.-> PVC2[PVC data-postgres-2]
    PVC0 --> PV0[PV\nEBS vol abc]
    PVC1 --> PV1[PV\nEBS vol def]
    PVC2 --> PV2[PV\nEBS vol ghi]
    P0 -.mounts.-> PVC0
    P1 -.mounts.-> PVC1
    P2 -.mounts.-> PVC2
    H[Headless Service\npostgres-headless\nclusterIP: None] -.DNS.-> P0
    H -.DNS.-> P1
    H -.DNS.-> P2
    Client[App client] --> DNS[postgres-0.postgres-headless.ns.svc]
    DNS --> P0
    SC[StorageClass\ngp3 SSD\nWaitForFirstConsumer] -.provisions.-> PV0
```

Key insight: `postgres-0` is always `postgres-0` across restarts. Its PVC `data-postgres-0` follows it. Its DNS name `postgres-0.postgres-headless.ns.svc.cluster.local` is stable. Replication protocols and leader election can address specific instances by name.

sections.title: The Three Guarantees That Only StatefulSets Provide
sections.content:
StatefulSets provide exactly three things Deployments do not.

**1. Stable network identity.** Pods get ordered, predictable names — `postgres-0, postgres-1, postgres-2` — that persist across restarts. Paired with a **headless Service** (`clusterIP: None`), each pod gets its own DNS entry: `postgres-0.postgres-headless.namespace.svc.cluster.local`. This lets replication protocols address specific instances by name.

**2. Stable persistent storage.** The `volumeClaimTemplates` field creates a separate PVC for each replica. Pod `postgres-0` gets PVC `data-postgres-0`, and this binding **survives pod deletion and rescheduling**. If `postgres-0` restarts on a different node, it reattaches to the same PVC — data follows it. Deployments sharing a single PVC would cause split-brain writes.

**3. Ordered operations.** StatefulSets create pods in order (0 then 1 then 2) and delete them in reverse (2 then 1 then 0). This is critical for databases where the primary must start first and establish leadership before replicas connect. Deployments start all pods simultaneously with no ordering guarantee.

**Operational complexity trade-off.** StatefulSet updates are sequential by default, making rollouts slower. **PVCs are NOT deleted when you delete the StatefulSet** — you must clean them up manually or accept the orphaned disk cost. This retention is intentional to prevent accidental data loss, but teams must plan for it. Use `reclaimPolicy: Retain` on the PersistentVolume for production so even PVC deletion does not destroy data.

sections.title: Managed Databases vs In-Cluster StatefulSets: The Production Decision
sections.content:
The existence of StatefulSets does not mean you should run databases in Kubernetes. For most Java backend teams, the right answer is **managed database services** — AWS RDS, Google Cloud SQL, Azure Database — for production data, and reserve StatefulSets for infrastructure that genuinely benefits from co-location.

**Managed databases handle:** backup scheduling with point-in-time recovery, failover orchestration, patch management, storage scaling, monitoring, read replicas. Running PostgreSQL in a StatefulSet means your team owns all of that: WAL archiving, scripted failover promotion, replication lag monitoring, storage performance tuning. Unless the team has dedicated DB operations expertise, this rarely justifies the co-location benefit.

**Where StatefulSets earn their complexity:**
- **Redis** as session store or cache — cluster-local latency matters, state tolerates restart.
- **Kafka** alongside microservices — avoids cross-network transfer costs, StatefulSet identity maps to broker ID.
- **Elasticsearch** co-located with log producers — reduces ingestion latency, stateful cluster membership.
- **Custom consensus-based services** (Consul, etcd, ZooKeeper) where clustered identity is baked in.

**StorageClass selection.** Use SSD-backed classes (`gp3` on AWS, `pd-ssd` on GCP) with **`volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer`** so the volume is provisioned in the same availability zone as the pod. Immediate binding can provision a volume in zone A while the pod is scheduled in zone B, causing `Pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims`.

**Backup must be separate from replication.** Replication is not backup. A `DROP TABLE` on the primary replicates instantly to every secondary. Use `pg_dump`, Velero, or cloud-provider snapshots scheduled independently, stored in a different account/region.

sections.title: Trade-offs, Ops Gotchas, and Alternatives
sections.content:
**PVC reclaim is asymmetric.** Create StatefulSet → PVCs created. Delete StatefulSet → **PVCs stay** (intentional). Scale down StatefulSet → **PVCs for removed replicas stay** (also intentional). This means every scale-down leaves orphaned disks until someone deletes them. Teams frequently accumulate hundreds of unused PVCs from scale events years old — real cloud cost.

**Scaling up is safe, scaling down is risky.** Adding `postgres-3` triggers replication catch-up. Removing `postgres-2` removes a replica — but if it was the primary, a failover is required first. Always manually promote before scale-down; StatefulSet scaling is not DB-aware.

**Operators are the real answer for databases.** If you must run PostgreSQL in Kubernetes, use an **operator** like Crunchy Postgres, CloudNativePG, or Zalando Postgres Operator. Operators know about primary/replica, handle failover, run backups, manage upgrades. A raw StatefulSet without an operator is a liability.

**Headless Service vs regular Service.** A StatefulSet usually needs both: a headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) for per-pod DNS (required for replication and leader election), plus a regular Service if clients want load balancing to any replica for read queries.

**Update strategy.** StatefulSet supports `RollingUpdate` (sequential, reverse order) and `OnDelete` (manual). For production databases prefer `OnDelete` so you control the order and timing of each replica restart; `RollingUpdate` can restart a primary before a replica is ready to take over.

**Costs to plan for.** Each PVC is a real cloud disk. 3 replicas × 100GB SSD × $0.10/GB-month ≈ $30/month per StatefulSet in storage alone. Scale events leave orphans. Production budgeting must account for this.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Most Spring Boot apps are stateless and belong on Deployments** — apps that use a database store their state externally; interchangeable replicas → Deployment.
- **StatefulSets provide stable identity: `postgres-0` survives restarts** — paired with headless Service (`clusterIP: None`), each pod has its own DNS for replication protocols.
- **VolumeClaimTemplates create one PVC per replica** — `data-postgres-0` binds exclusively to pod `postgres-0` and follows across rescheduling; sharing a PVC in a Deployment causes split-brain writes.
- **Deleting a StatefulSet does not delete its PVCs** — prevents accidental data loss but creates orphaned disks if not planned; use `reclaimPolicy: Retain` on production volumes.
- **Prefer managed databases for production data** — RDS / Cloud SQL handle backup, failover, patching; reserve StatefulSets for co-located infrastructure like Redis, Kafka, Elasticsearch where cluster-local latency matters.
- **Use `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer`** — ensures the PV is provisioned in the same zone as the scheduled pod; immediate binding can strand pods with unbound PVCs across zones.
- **Scaling down leaves PVCs; monitor and clean** — orphaned PVCs accumulate cloud cost; add ops runbook for post-scale-down cleanup or use an operator.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Persistent Volumes and StatefulSets together solve running stateful workloads in Kubernetes — databases or message brokers that need durable storage and stable network identity across Pod restarts.

**Persistent Volumes — storage abstraction**
- A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) requests storage by size and access mode (`ReadWriteOnce`, `ReadWriteMany`); Kubernetes binds it to a PersistentVolume either pre-provisioned by an admin or dynamically created by a StorageClass.
- `ReadWriteOnce` means only one node can mount the volume at a time — the constraint for most block storage (AWS EBS, GCE Persistent Disk); a StatefulSet with 3 replicas and `ReadWriteOnce` means each replica gets its own PVC, not one shared.
- The PVC lifecycle is independent of the Pod — delete the Pod or even the StatefulSet and the PVC (and the data) survive; explicitly delete the PVC to release storage; this is intentional for durability.

**StatefulSet — ordered, stable pods**
- StatefulSets give each pod a stable identity: `db-0, db-1, db-2`; the DNS name for `db-0` is `db-0.db-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local` — this stability is what PostgreSQL, Kafka, Elasticsearch require for cluster membership and leader election.
- StatefulSets scale and update in order: `db-0` starts before `db-1`; during a rolling update `db-2` updates first, then `db-1`, then `db-0` — this ensures the primary (usually `db-0`) is updated last, minimizing failover window.
- `volumeClaimTemplates` automatically creates a PVC for each pod; `db-0` gets `data-db-0` and restarting `db-0` always reattaches to the same volume.

**When to use StatefulSets**
- Use Deployments for stateless Spring Boot services — simpler, roll back more cleanly, no PVCs needed.
- Use StatefulSets for databases (if running in Kubernetes at all), Kafka brokers, Elasticsearch nodes, or any process requiring stable network identity or per-instance durable storage.
- Most teams run databases outside Kubernetes on managed services (RDS, Cloud Spanner) — the operational complexity of StatefulSets and storage is worth avoiding when a managed service handles it.

**Operational gotchas**
- Scaling down a StatefulSet removes pods but leaves PVCs — orphaned disks accumulate cloud cost over time; add a cleanup runbook or use an operator.
- Use `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` on the StorageClass so volumes are provisioned in the same availability zone as the scheduled pod.
- Replication is not backup — a `DROP TABLE` replicates instantly; schedule `pg_dump` or snapshots stored in a different region/account for real durability.
